source.title: What Can Transformer Learn with Varying Depth? Case Studies on Sequence Learning Tasks

record.tranche_reason: Tests memorization of randomly assigned labels in a different setting: synthetic sequences and attention-only transformers, with theoretical constructions and training experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper studies synthetic sequence classification, not image labeling. Its labels are randomly permuted across examples, but it does not report test error or compare true-label generalization. It also studies an attention-only architecture and uses task-specific initializations for several experiments. No results test V2–V6. Figure curves are not numerically recoverable from the supplied text.
record.test_reason: The study trains attention-only transformers with SGD on randomly assigned sequence labels and reports memorization results, testing V1 in a new synthetic setting. Its theoretical construction alone does not test SGD fitting.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate: one attention layer suffices for their memorization task, whereas their reasoning and template-generalization tasks require at least two. Three layers suffice for contextual generalization; necessity of three is suggested experimentally but not proved.
record.recipe_differences: Synthetic sequence classification rather than image classification; attention-only transformer; theoretical existence construction and synthetic SGD experiments; no test-error measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: Number of attention heads affects how easily the model memorizes in the reported experiment.

fits_no_version.finding: A constructed one-layer attention-only transformer can classify every sequence in the distinct-label task correctly.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A single attention layer with sufficient heads and embedding dimensions has representational capacity to memorize distinct sequence labels.

record.problems: The reported experiments use synthetic sequences and random permuted distinct labels, with no test-error or true-label comparison. The theoretical theorem is an existence result. Exact experimental outcomes are displayed in figures without recoverable numeric values in the supplied text. Several non-memorization experiments use task-specific constructed initialization.

untested.parts: Chance-level test error and fitting with architecture and hyperparameters unchanged relative to true-label training. The labeling scheme uses distinct classes for every example rather than independent assignments to a fixed shared class set.
Training-time comparison between true and random labels, and convergence as label corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and steadily degrading test performance across label-corruption fractions.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and augmentation on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
Learning shared real-data patterns before memorizing noise.

record.verdict_notes: Neither untested parts of V1 nor improved learning with more heads justifies the record's limits_scope labels. The qualitative memorization findings are consistent with V1, but the supplied text does not establish its zero-or-near-zero training-error criterion sufficiently to assign a verdict. Image inputs are not an explicit requirement of V1.

versions.untested_parts: Image inputs, test error at chance, comparison with true-label generalization, and fitting without changing architecture or training hyperparameters.

any dataset of the sequence classification task

rows.value: TF(X) = y for all (X, y) in the dataset
rows.note: Theoretical existence result, not evidence of optimization by stochastic gradient methods or test performance.
rows.check: Theorem 5.1 establishes existence of suitable weights, independently of training. It does not establish that stochastic gradient training finds them. Retain as a capacity result rather than empirical evidence for V1.

rows.subject: single-layer transformer (trained experimental model; specific checkpoint not stated)
rows.size_stated: 1 layer; hidden size 508; head count varied in Appendix B.2
rows.operation_detail: Trained on synthetic sequence-classification examples with randomly permuted distinct labels using SGD.
rows.value: Figure 2 shows training curves; authors state that a single-layer transformer performs well on the memorization task.
rows.note: Figure contains curves for the listed dataset sizes, but exact endpoint values are not stated. The setup says examples receive random permuted distinct labels; test performance is not reported.
rows.check: The text reports successful memorization qualitatively, but the supplied figure transcription does not reveal training-accuracy endpoints. Neither near-zero error nor clearly incomplete fitting can be established, so 'partial' is unsupported. Labels are a random permutation of e distinct classes, one class per example. Inputs contain six tokens plus the appended response sign.

source_check.locator_found: Section 6.1 and Figure 2; Appendix B.1, experimental model, data and training setup.

rows.subject: 1-layer transformer, head count varied
rows.operation_detail: Compared training dynamics on the memorization task while varying the number of attention heads.
rows.measure: training accuracy and loss over training steps
rows.baseline: single-layer models with different head counts are compared
rows.value: Authors state that increasing the number of attention heads allows the model to more easily memorize the data; Figure 5 shows the training dynamics.
rows.note: The exact curve values are not stated. This result concerns training dynamics, not test error.
rows.check: The authors report easier memorization with additional heads, but readable endpoint accuracies are unavailable. This does not establish incomplete fitting or failure for any head count. It also does not test V2, which requires comparison with true-label training or varying corruption fractions.
